title: "We can make a big change:" Local residents react to IURC report - NewsBreak
text:
By Ian Young De’Onta Bush ,
1 hours ago
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WEHT) — Indiana has released its energy affordability plan outlining both short and long-term plans to address the rising cost of energy.
The report has received reaction from both state officials and residents, with people in the Hoosier state saying they want relief now.
“If all of us come together, we can make a big change,” says Newburgh resident Jonathan Ellerbusch. “Honestly, in my opinion, numbers mean a lot, and I think the numbers produced with our voices, that’s another big thing we can do.”
The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission has compiled a report from 10 listening sessions where people are asking for legislative action and investigations into utility profit and billing. Customers say they want the following:
Programs using shareholder dollars to help with customer assistance Utilities to evaluate energy efficiency programs Communicate clearly with customers “If that’s what they’re going to do, let’s see it,” says Evansville resident Ricky Underhill. “You mean because, like I said, it’s getting ridiculous. So, let’s see some kind of end results for the customers who have been paying.”
State officials are reacting, with representative Alex Burton saying Hoosiers are refusing to be lullabied and distracted away from addressing our energy cost burden.
State Rep. Alex Burton reacts to IURC Energy Affordability Report Governor Mike Braun calls the report a great step to making energy bills more affordable. He says Hoosier families work hard to make every dollar count, and utility companies must start doing the same.
Residents say one thing in the report stuck out to them: the possibility of removing the 7% sales tax on utilities.
“I’d be very happy about it, genuinely, because I don’t believe that we’re getting more taxes on top of everything that we have now,” says Evansville resident Cyrous Baker. “I think it’s the biggest for the country. Yeah. And for the state here.”
“Getting rid of that tax would be kind of cool because that would probably cut back quite a bit on utilities for people that could use that towards groceries or, you know, even just buying things for themselves,” says Ellerbusch.
CenterPoint Energy says that they are determined to work with the in-state peer utilities and other stakeholders to do even more to build an affordable and reliable energy future.
